title: The first WTTW shows and a payment dispute
summary: Hodes took his jazz talk to WTTW, which had no money. A year later they paid him scale.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: But I knew that I could do it with playing. But I still hadn't had it all together. Like, these schools got it all together for me. I even played for high school kids. In many halls, you're sitting with -- the back of your head is facing them, 200 kids all around you. And you can feel a tomato flying through the air. And -- boom. But it never happened, and I built this little thing on jazz, and I brought it to WTTW, and did it and they liked it, but they couldn't give me no money. I says, I don't work for free. So I'll see you.
Maybe we should explain that WTTW is an educational --

Is an educational station. They didn't have the money. So I says, that's okay, could I have the tape? Says, oh, sure. Guy was very friendly, still one of my best friends, Bob Kaiser. So it wasn't his doing, they just didn't have the money. They gave me the tapes, I took them home.
And it was about a year later, they found enough money to pay me what the union scale was to do it. So I came back and did it again. And then they got interested in me
doing it with a band. And they had this guy, Rubenstein, Marty Rubenstein, kind of interviewing me and talking to me, the new and the old.
Yeah, he's a very fine pianist, too.

Yeah, very fine. And he sat and talked to me about jazz and we played, and I had Brunis and the regular guys. And that we got paid -- everybody got paid something and it was shown, wow. So then the station moved to 5200 North from the South, and time passed, and again, the opportunity came to us to do a show, alone.
